title: Rebar
subtitle: Making AI construction takeoffs trustworthy, starting with scale

hero.alt: Rebar plan editor with the consolidated calibration popover

overview: Rebar is an AI-powered takeoff platform for mechanical and HVAC contractors. Estimators upload construction plan sets and Rebar's AI extracts the measurements, schedules, and quantities they'd otherwise count by hand, turning days of manual takeoff into minutes.

But an AI number is only useful if the estimator believes it. And every measurement Rebar produces rests on one fragile input: the scale of each sheet. Get scale wrong and every downstream quantity is wrong, quietly.

This case study is about the least glamorous, highest-leverage part of that trust problem: calibration. It consolidated scale from three scattered surfaces into one, and set the pattern for how we surface AI confidence across the product.

outcomes.label: Faster to set and verify scale

sections.label: Challenge
sections.headline: AI takeoffs are only as trustworthy as the scale underneath them.
sections.subheading: Estimators wouldn't rely on Rebar until they could trust and verify it:

cards.text: Every quantity depends on sheet scale. One mis-scaled page silently corrupts the whole takeoff.
When the AI detected scale, there was no clear way to see where a number came from or whether to trust it.
Scale controls lived in three disconnected places, so there was no single source of truth.
A wrong number an estimator can't catch is worse than no number at all. Trust, once broken, doesn't come back.

cards.title: High-stakes, low-margin
cards.description: A bid won or lost on a bad quantity is real money. Estimators are accountable for every number.

cards.title: Varied tech comfort
cards.description: From spreadsheet veterans to first-week hires. The workflow has to be obvious, not clever.

cards.title: Skeptical of black boxes
cards.description: They've been burned by automation before. They trust what they can see and correct, not what they're told.

problems.title: Scale lived in three places
problems.description: Setting or correcting scale meant hunting across a toolbar Scale + DPI menu, a 'saved scales' dropdown on the scale chip, and a per-page floor-plans list. Each showed a slice of the truth; none showed all of it.

quote.text: I could never remember where the scale setting actually was. Every project felt like a scavenger hunt.
quote.author: [Estimator name, Company]

problems.title: No source of truth
problems.description: With controls scattered, estimators couldn't answer a basic question: what scale is this sheet, and where did that scale come from: the AI, a default, or me?

problems.title: AI scale was invisible when it was wrong
problems.description: When the AI mis-detected a scale, nothing surfaced it. The error only showed up downstream as a quantity that looked off, long after the estimator had moved on.

quote.text: I don't need it to be perfect. I need to know when it's not sure, so I can check.
quote.author: [Estimator name, Company]

features.name: One place for scale
features.headline: Every scale, one popover.
features.description: I consolidated all three surfaces into a single calibration popover. It answers the whole question at a glance: what scale each sheet is, and where it came from. Setting, correcting, and reviewing scale now happen in one predictable place.

features.name: Defaults that cascade
features.headline: Set it once, override where it matters.
features.description: A document and project default covers the common case, with per-floor-plan overrides for the sheets that differ. Estimators stop re-setting the same scale page after page and only touch the exceptions.

media.alt: Document and project defaults with per-floor-plan rows

features.name: Show the work
features.headline: Where every scale came from.
features.description: Each sheet shows whether its scale was AI-detected, inherited from a default, or set by hand. Low-confidence detections are flagged with a plain-language bucket, not a percentage, so estimators know exactly where to look before they trust a number.

sections.title: Iterations
sections.headline: Hardened in QA and early use.

items.title: Explicit cross-page propagation
items.description: Applying a scale across pages used to happen silently. We made propagation visible and intentional, so estimators always know which sheets a change touched.

items.title: Calmer picker interaction
items.description: Reworked how the scale picker opens so setting scale on a page felt inline and predictable instead of modal and disruptive.

items.title: Confidence, refined
items.description: Tuned the low-confidence threshold and language after watching where estimators actually double-checked, so the flag earns attention instead of crying wolf.

items.title: Trust is a design surface.
items.description: For AI features, showing provenance and uncertainty isn't polish. It's the product. Estimators adopt what they can verify.

items.title: Confidence is a bucket, not a number.
items.description: 'Low confidence, check this' beats '73%.' Named buckets tell people what to do; percentages make them do math.

items.title: Removing surfaces is a feature.
items.description: The win wasn't new controls. It was collapsing three into one and giving scale a single, obvious home.

items.title: Design for the 90% path.
items.description: Estimators aren't power users. Defaults that cascade beat flexibility no one asked for.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.headline: From scattered setting to a source of truth.
paragraphs: Calibration went from three disconnected controls to one popover that sets, corrects, and explains scale in a single place. Estimators can finally answer 'what scale is this, and can I trust it?' without leaving their flow.

More than a cleanup, it set the trust pattern for the rest of Rebar: show where an AI number came from, flag when we're unsure in plain language, and always leave the estimator in control. That's how a takeoff tool earns the right to be believed.
